summary: North Macedonia is a landlocked country in the central Balkan Peninsula. It became independent from Yugoslavia in 1991 and adopted its present name after reaching an agreement with Greece in 2019, and is known for Lake Ohrid.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: In the late 9th century Saint Clement and Saint Naum established a Slavic Christian center at Ohrid, and Orthodoxy has since been the faith of the Macedonian Slavs. During Ottoman rule the Orthodox Church was an important organization maintaining Slavic identity. In 1967 the Macedonian Orthodox Church declared autocephaly from the Serbian Church, and for a long time it was not recognized by other Orthodox churches, being recognized only in 2022. Today Orthodox Christians are mainly ethnic Macedonians.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam arrived after the Ottoman conquest in the late 14th century, and most Albanians and Turks, as well as some Slavs (called Torbeši or Macedonian Muslims), converted to Islam. Today Muslims live mainly in the Albanian-populated areas of the west such as Tetovo and Gostivar, and their proportion is rising because of a higher birth rate.

ranking.name: Other Christianity
ranking.description: These include Catholicism (mainly Albanians and some Eastern Catholics), other Christian denominations such as Protestantism, and those who did not declare a religion.

religion.background: Christianity reached the Macedonian region in the 1st century, in the time of the apostle Paul; in the 9th century Saint Clement and Saint Naum, disciples of Saints Cyril and Methodius, established a center of Slavic literature at Ohrid, which became an important center of Orthodoxy. At the end of the 14th century the Ottoman Empire conquered Macedonia and ruled for more than five hundred years, during which some Slavs and most Albanians and Turks converted to Islam. After the Balkan Wars of 1913, Macedonia was divided among Serbia, Greece and Bulgaria, and the area of present-day North Macedonia belonged to Serbia and later Yugoslavia. In 1967 the Macedonian Orthodox Church declared autocephaly, and it was recognized by the Ecumenical Patriarchate only in 2022. After the armed conflict of ethnic Albanians in 2001, the Ohrid Agreement guaranteed the rights of ethnic Albanians.

language.official: Macedonian is the official language, and Albanian is also a nationwide official language.

ranking.name: Macedonian
ranking.description: Macedonian was formally standardized after the founding of the Republic of Macedonia in Yugoslavia in 1944, becoming the language of the state and education. Since Bulgaria has long maintained that Macedonian is a dialect of Bulgarian, the language issue remains a sensitive matter between the two countries and has even affected North Macedonia's negotiations to join the European Union.

ranking.name: Albanian
ranking.description: Albanians have lived in western Macedonia since the Middle Ages, and their numbers grew in the Ottoman period. After the 2001 armed conflict of ethnic Albanians, the Ohrid Agreement provided that a language spoken by more than 20 percent of the population could become an official language locally, and a 2019 law raised Albanian to a nationwide official language. Albanian is used mainly in places such as Tetovo and Gostivar in the west.

ranking.name: Turkish
ranking.description: Turkish is a language left by more than five hundred years of Ottoman rule, and ethnic Turks live mainly in cities and some villages in the east. In the 20th century many Turks moved to Turkey and their numbers fell, but Turkish remains one of the local official languages in some areas.

ranking.name: Romani
ranking.description: The Roma moved into the Balkans from India in the late Middle Ages via the Byzantine and Ottoman empires. Šuto Orizari in North Macedonia is the first municipality in the world with a Roma majority and a Roma mayor, and Romani has official status there.

language.history: Macedonian belongs to the South Slavic branch and is very close to Bulgarian. In the 9th century Saints Cyril and Methodius created the Glagolitic alphabet, and their disciples developed the early Cyrillic alphabet at Ohrid. During Ottoman rule the Macedonian region used many languages, and in the 19th century both Bulgaria and Serbia claimed that the Macedonian Slavs belonged to their own nation. After the founding of the Socialist Republic of Macedonia in Yugoslavia in 1944, Macedonian was formally standardized on the basis of the western dialects and became the official language. After the renaming to North Macedonia in 2019, Albanian also gained official status at the national level.

ranking.name: Tavče gravče (baked beans)
ranking.description: White beans stewed in a clay pot with onion and paprika and then baked in the oven, the national dish of North Macedonia. It has a creamy texture with the aroma of paprika and onion and is often eaten with bread.
ranking.history: Tavče gravče means "beans in a pan" and uses the large white beans grown in North Macedonia, baked in a traditional clay pot (tavče). Beans are an important source of protein for Balkan farmers, and during the fasts of the Orthodox Church, believers who may not eat meat also often take bean dishes as a staple. Today it is the signature dish of North Macedonian homes and restaurants, often eaten on Fridays and during fasts.

ranking.name: Ajvar
ranking.description: A spread made by peeling and mashing roasted red bell peppers and eggplant, then slowly cooking them with garlic, oil and salt, spread on bread.
ranking.history: The name ajvar comes from the Turkish havyar (caviar); in the 19th century the Serbs used this name for a kind of caviar, and it later came to refer to red pepper relish. Peppers are native to the Americas and came to the Balkans via the Ottoman Empire after the 16th century. Each autumn when the peppers are harvested, households across North Macedonia roast peppers in their yards and cook ajvar for winter, a seasonal activity in which the community and family take part together.

ranking.name: Pastrmajlija
ranking.description: An oval bread made from fermented dough, topped with pieces of cured pork or lamb and eggs and baked. The crust is crisp and the meat salty and savory, a local specialty snack.
ranking.history: The name pastrmajlija comes from pastrma, cured dried meat, which spread through the Balkans and Anatolia in Ottoman times. It is the signature food of Štip in central North Macedonia, which holds a pastrmajlija festival each year. It is called the "Macedonian pizza" and is often eaten with pickled peppers and a yogurt drink.

ranking.name: Burek
ranking.description: A flaky pastry pie of many thin layers of dough filled with cheese, minced meat or spinach and baked, often eaten with yogurt for breakfast. The crust is crisp and the fillings varied, and it is the most common breakfast in North Macedonia.
ranking.history: Burek comes from the Ottoman börek, generally thought to be related to the noodle and dough traditions of the Turkic peoples of Central Asia, and entered the Balkans with the Ottoman Empire after the 14th century. In North Macedonia burek is the most common breakfast, with bakeries selling it from early morning, served with a glass of yogurt drink. It is one of the culinary legacies of five hundred years of Ottoman rule.

ranking.name: Shopska salad
ranking.description: A salad of diced tomato, cucumber, onion and pepper, topped with plenty of grated white cheese. It is refreshing, with the saltiness of the cheese and the light sweetness of the vegetables complementing each other.
ranking.history: Shopska salad is generally thought to have been designed in the 1950s–60s by the Bulgarian state tourism company to promote tourism, its red, green and white colors symbolizing the Bulgarian flag, and its name coming from the Shopi people of western Bulgaria. In the socialist period it spread across the Balkans through tourism and exchange with Yugoslavia, and in North Macedonia it is likewise a salad ordered before every meal, eaten with the strong spirit rakija.
